lo.e: From Middle English lo, loo, from Old English lā (“exclamation of surprise, grief, or joy”). Conflated in Middle English with lo! (interjection), a corruption of lok!, loke! (“look!”) (as in lo we! (look we!)).
lo.g: look, see, behold (in an imperative sense).

load.e: The sense of “burden” first arose in the 13th century as a secondary meaning of Middle English lode, loade, which had the main significance of “way, course, journey”, from Old English lād (“course, journey; way, street, waterway; leading, carrying.
load.g: A burden; a weight to be carried.

load.e: Acronym of living online all day.
load.g: A person that spends all day online. The term was originally used in the late 1980s to describe users on free Q-Link (later America Online)

loaden.e: From Middle English *loden, lode, variant of laden, y-lade, from Old English hladen, ġehladen (“loaded, laden”), equivalent to load + -en (past participle ending).

loading.g: The process by which something is loaded.

loaf.e: From Middle English laf, lof, loof, from Old English hlāf (“bread; loaf”), from Proto-West Germanic *hlaib, from Proto-Germanic *hlaibaz (“bread; loaf”), of uncertain origin. Perhaps related to Old English hlifian (“to stand out prominently, tower up”).
loaf.g: A block of bread after baking.
To do nothing, to be idle.

loan.e: From Middle English lone, lane, from Old Norse lán, from Proto-Germanic *laihną, from Proto-Indo-European *leykʷ- (“to leave (over)”).
loan.g: An act or instance of lending, an act or instance of granting something for temporary use.

loan.e: From Scottish Gaelic lòn (“marshy meadow”) (compare lèana (“wet meadow, marsh, meadow”)).
loan.g: An area of uncultivated ground near a village or farmhouse.

loathe.e: From Middle English lothe, from Old English lāþian, from Proto-West Germanic *laiþēn, from Proto-Germanic *laiþāną.
loathe.g: To detest, hate, or revile (someone or something).

loathing.g: Sense of revulsion, distaste, detestation, extreme hatred or dislike.

loathsome.e: From Middle English lothsum, from Old English *lāþsum, from Proto-West Germanic *laiþasam, equivalent to loath + -some.

loave.e: From Middle English lof, from Old English lof (“praise, glory, repute”).
From Middle English loven, from Old English lofian (“to praise, exalt, appraise, value”).

lobe.e: From Middle French lobe in early 16th century, from New Latin lobus (“a lobe”), from Ancient Greek λοβός (lobós, “the lobe of the ear or of the liver, the pod of a leguminous plant”).
lobe.g: Any projection or division, especially one of a somewhat rounded form.

locate.e: Borrowed from Latin locātus, perfect passive participle of locō (“to place”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from locus (“place”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix).
locate.g: To place; to set in a particular spot or position.

location.e: Borrowed from Latin locatio, locationis (“a placing”), from locare (“to place, put, set, let”), from locus (“a place”). Equivalent to locate + -ion.
location.g: A particular point or place in physical space.

lock.e: From Middle English lok, from Old English loc, from Proto-West Germanic *lok, from Proto-Germanic *luką from Proto-Indo-European *lewg- (“to bend; turn”).
lock.g: Something used for fastening, which can only be opened with a key or combination.

lock.e: From Middle English lok, lokke, from Old English locc (“hair of the head, hair, lock of hair, curl, ringlet”), from Proto-West Germanic *lokk, from Proto-Germanic *lukkaz, from Proto-Indo-European *lugnó-, from Proto-Indo-European *lewg- (“to bend”).
lock.g: A tuft or length of hair, wool, etc.

locked.g: Having undergone locking; secured by a lock.

locust.e: From Middle English locuste, locust, from Anglo-Norman locuste, Middle French locuste, and their source, Latin locusta (“locust, crustacean, lobster”).
locust.g: Any of the grasshoppers, often polyphenic and usually swarming, in the family Acrididae that are very destructive to crops and other vegetat

lodge.e: From Middle English logge, from Old French loge (“an arbour, a covered walk-way”).
lodge.g: A building for recreational use such as a hunting lodge or a summer cabin.

loft.e: From Middle English lofte (“air, sky, upper region, loft”), from Old English loft, (doublet of native Old English lyft) of North Germanic origin, from Old Norse lopt (“upper chamber, attic, region of sky, air”), from Proto-Germanic *luftuz (“air, sky”).
loft.g: Air, the air; the sky, the heavens.

lofty.e: From Middle English lofty, lofti, lofte (“of high rank; noble; ornate”), equivalent to loft (“sky, firmament; upper room”) + -y.
lofty.g: High, tall, having great height or stature.

log.e: From Middle English logge, logg (first recorded in Anglo-Latin as loggum), of uncertain origin, but probably from Old Norse lóg, lág (“felled tree, log”), derived from Old Norse liggja (“to lie”). If so, then cognate with Norwegian låg (“fallen tree”), Dutch loog (“wood, timber, lumber”).
log.g: The trunk of a dead tree, cleared of branches.

log.e: Clipping of logbook, itself from log (etymology 1) + book, from a wooden float (chip log) used to measure speed.
log.g: A logbook, or journal of a vessel's (or aircraft's) progress.

loin.e: From Middle English loyne, from Old French loigne, from Vulgar Latin *lumbea, from Latin lumbus, of uncertain origin, possibly from Oscan-Umbrian *londwo- or Proto-Germanic *lundwuz, both ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *lendʰ- (“kidney, waist”).
loin.g: The part of the body (of humans and quadrupeds) at each side of the backbone, between the ribs and hips.

loincloth.g: A garment worn about the loins and covering the crotch.

lonely.e: From lone + -ly, or from an apheretic shortening of alonely.
lonely.g: Unhappy due to feeling isolated from contact with other people.

long.e: From Middle English long, lang, from Old English long, lang (“long, tall, lasting”), from Proto-West Germanic *lang, from Proto-Germanic *langaz (“long”), from Proto-Indo-European *dlongʰos (“long”).
long.g: Having much distance in space from one end to the other.

long.e: From Middle English long, lang, an aphetic form of Middle English ilong, ylong, from Old English ġelong, ġelang (“along, belonging, depending, consequent”); the verb later reinterpreted as an aphetic form of belong.

long-winded.g: Tediously long in speaking; consuming much time; unnecessarily verbose.

longing.e: From Middle English longynge, langynge, langand, from Old English langiende, from Proto-Germanic *langōndz, present participle of Proto-Germanic *langōną (“to desire, long for”), equivalent to long + -ing (present participle ending).

look.e: From Middle English loken, lokien, from Old English lōcian, from Proto-West Germanic *lōkōn. Further origin unknown, no certain cognates outside Germanic. Likely also related to German lugen (“to peek”), Alemannic German luege (“to look”), Yiddish לוגן (lugn).
look.g: To try to see, to pay attention to with one’s eyes.

looking.e: From Middle English lokynge, from earlier lokinde, lokende, from Old English lōciende, present participle of Old English lōcian (“to look”), equivalent to look + -ing.

lookout.g: A vantage point with a view of the surrounding area.

loom.e: From Middle English lome, from Old English *lōma, ġelōma (“tool, utensil, implement, article of furniture, household effect”) (also as andlōma, andġelōma, andlama (“utensil, instrument, implement, tool, vessel”), from Proto-West Germanic *lōmō, *lamō (“tool, utensil”), of uncertain origin.
loom.g: A utensil; tool; a weapon; (usually in compound) an article in general.

loom.e: Shetland dialect, denoting a diver or guillemot, from Old Norse lómr, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *leh₂- (“to howl”) (expressive root).

loop.e: From Middle English loupe (“noose, loop”), earlier lowp-knot (“loop-knot”), of North Germanic origin, from Old Norse hlaup (“a run”), used in the sense of a "running knot", from hlaupa (“to leap”), ultimately from Proto-Germanic *hlaupaną (“to leap, run”).
loop.g: A length of thread, line or rope that is doubled over to make an opening.

loose.e: From Middle English loos, los, lous, from Old Norse lauss, from Proto-Germanic *lausaz, whence also -less, leasing; from Proto-Indo-European *lewh₁- (“to untie, set free, separate”), whence also lyo-, -lysis, via Ancient Greek.
loose.g: To let loose, to free from restraints.

loot.e: Borrowed from Hindi लूट (lūṭ, “booty”), either from Sanskrit लोप्त्र (loptra, “booty, stolen property”) or लुण्ट् (luṇṭ, “to rob, plunder”). The figurative meaning developed in American English in the 1920s, resulting in a generalized meaning by the 1950s.
loot.g: Synonym of booty, goods seized from an enemy by violence, particularly (historical) during the sacking of a town in war or (video games) aft

loot.e: Borrowed from Middle Dutch loet or loete (“scoop, shovel, scraper”), from reconstructed Old Dutch *lōta, from Old Frankish *lōtija (“scoop”), from Proto-Germanic *hlōþþijō (“scoop”), from Proto-Indo-European *kleh₂- (“to lay down, deposit, overlay”).
loot.g: A scoop used to remove scum from brine pans in saltworks.

lop.e: From Middle English loppe (“bough”); the verb is a back-formation from the noun.
lop.g: To cut off as the top or extreme part of anything, especially to prune a small limb off a shrub or tree, or sometimes to behead someone.

lop.e: From Middle English loppe (“flea, spider”), from Old English loppe (“spider, silk-worm, flea”), from Proto-Germanic *luppǭ (“flea, sandflea", originally, "jumper”), from Proto-Germanic *luppijaną (“to jump, dart”).

lord.e: From Middle English lord and lorde (attested from the 15th century), from earlier (14th century) lourde and other variants which dropped the intervocalic consonant of earlier lowerd, louerd, loverd, laford, and lhoaverd; from Old English hlāford < hlāfweard, a compound of hlāf (“bread”) + weard (“guardian”); see loaf and ward.
lord.g: The master of the servants of a household; (historical) the master of a feudal manor

lordly.e: From Middle English lordly, lordlich, from Old English hlāfordlīċ (“lordly; heroic; noble”), equivalent to lord + -ly (forming adjectives).
lordly.g: Of or relating to a lord.

lordly.e: From Middle English lordly, lordely, lordliche, equivalent to lord + -ly (forming adverbs).
lordly.g: In the manner of a lord. Showing command or nobility.

lordship.e: From Middle English lordschipe, from Old English hlāfordsċiepe, equivalent to lord + -ship.
lordship.g: The state or condition of being a lord.

lose.e: From Middle English losen, from Old English losian. The modern pronunciation with /uː/ (instead of the /oʊ~əʊ/ that would be expected from Early Modern /ɔː/) is due to conflation with loose.
lose.g: To cease to have (something) in one's possession or capability.

loss.e: From Middle English los, from Old English los (“damage, destruction, loss”), from Proto-West Germanic *los, from Proto-Germanic *lusą (“dissolution, break-up, loss”), from Proto-Indo-European *lews- (“to cut, sunder, separate, loose, lose”).
loss.g: The result of no longer possessing an object, a function, or a characteristic due to external causes or misplacement.

loss.e: Pronunciation spelling of lost, representing African-American Vernacular English.

lost.e: From Middle English loste, losede (preterite) and Middle English lost, ilost, ilosed (past participle), from Old English losode (preterite) and Old English losod, ġelosod, equivalent to lose + -t.
lost.g: Having wandered from, or unable to find, the way.

lot.e: From Middle English lot, from Old English hlot (“portion, choice, decision”), from Proto-West Germanic *hlut, from Proto-Germanic *hlutą. Related also to German Los.
lot.g: A large quantity or number; a great deal.

lotus.e: Borrowed from Latin lōtus, from Ancient Greek λωτός (lōtós). Ultimately from Hebrew לוֹט (lōṭ, “myrrh”, literally “covering, envelope”).
lotus.g: Any member of the genus Nelumbo of aquatic plants in the family Nelumbonaceae.

loud.e: From Middle English loude, loud, lud, from Old English hlūd (“loud, noisy, sounding, sonorous”), from Proto-West Germanic *hlūd, from Proto-Germanic *hlūdaz, *hlūþaz (“heard”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱlewtos (“heard, famous”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱlew- (“to hear”).
From Middle English loude, from Old English hlūde (“loudly”), from Proto-Germanic *hlūda, *hlūdô (“loudly”), related to Etymology 1.

loudly.e: From Middle English loudly, equivalent to loud + -ly.
loudly.g: In a loud manner; at a high volume.

lounge.e: Origin uncertain. Perhaps borrowed from French s'allonger (“to lie down”).
lounge.g: To relax; to spend time lazily; to stand, sit, or recline, in an indolent manner.

love.e: From Middle English love, luve, from Old English lufu, from Proto-West Germanic *lubu, from Proto-Germanic *lubō, from Proto-Indo-European *lewbʰ- (“love, care, desire”). The close of a letter sense is presumably a truncation of With love or the like. Eclipsed non-native English amour (“love”), borrowed from Norman amour (“love”).
love.g: A deep caring for the existence of another.

love.e: The verb sense is from Middle English loven, luvien, from Old English lufian (“to love”), from Proto-West Germanic *lubōn (“to love”), derived from the noun.
love.g: To have a strong affection for (someone or something).

loved.e: From Middle English loved, luvd, from Old English lufode, first and third person singular past indicative of lufian; and Middle English loved, iloved, from Old English ġelufod, past participle of lufian; both equivalent to love + -ed.

lovely.e: From Middle English lovely, luvelich, lufli, from Old English luflīċ, luflīc (“amiable, loving, lovable”), equivalent to love + -ly.
lovely.g: Delightful for beauty, harmony, or grace.

lovely.e: From Middle English lofly, lovely (“praiseworthy; laudatory”), equivalent to lofe + -ly.

lover.e: From Middle English lovere, luffer, lufere, equivalent to love + -er.
lover.g: One who loves and cares for another person in a romantic way; a sweetheart, love, soulmate, boyfriend, girlfriend, or spouse.

loving.e: From Middle English lovyng(e) (“love”), inherited from Old English lufung. By surface analysis, love + -ing.
loving.g: The action of the verb to love.

lovingkindness.e: From loving + kindness. The word arises in the King James Version of the Bible as a translation of Hebrew חסד (ḥeseḏ, “grace, kindness, love; chesed”).
lovingkindness.g: Kindness or mercy which is based on, or arises from, love; (countable) an act of such kindness or mercy.

low.e: From Middle English lough, from Old English hlōh, first and third person singular preterite of hliehhan (“to laugh”).

lower.g: To let descend by its own weight, as something suspended; to let down.

lowly.e: From low + -ly; compare Middle English lowly.
lowly.g: Not high; not elevated in place; low.

loyal.e: Borrowed from Middle French loyal, from Old French loial, leial, leal, from Latin lēgālis.
loyal.g: Having or demonstrating undivided and constant support for someone or something.

loyalty.e: From Middle English loialte, borrowed from Old French loialte, loiauté (Modern loyauté) from loial + -té, equivalent to loyal + -ty.
loyalty.g: The state of being loyal; fidelity.
